title: Gravitational waves detected
reading: On 14 September 2015, two detectors in the United States, each with arms four kilometres long, register a passing ripple in space-time. It changes the length of each arm by less than a thousandth of the diameter of a proton — a fractional strain of about 10⁻²¹. The signal matches the prediction of general relativity for two black holes, each roughly thirty times the mass of the sun, spiralling together and merging more than a billion light-years away. The waves Professor Einstein predicted in 1916 are real, and they are now a new way of observing the universe.
detail: Black holes: regions of space-time from which light cannot escape, following from Schwarzschild's 1916 solution; the name dates from the 1960s. In 1936 Einstein and Rosen briefly concluded that gravitational waves do not exist, before correcting the error.

claim.label: I did not expect detection
claim.summary: Einstein predicted gravitational waves in 1916 and gave the quadrupole formula in 1918; he considered their effects too small to have practical significance. He had not doubted them in 1927; the 1936 doubt lies in his future.
voice: I predicted them in 1916 and calculated in 1918 how much energy a system radiates in this way. I concluded the effects were so small they could have no practical significance. A thousandth of a proton over four kilometres — I would not have believed anyone could measure that. I am delighted to have been wrong about the practical part.
claim.reasoning: Confirmation of his own theory at a precision he thought impossible.

historical.note: Einstein did not live to see indirect evidence (the Hulse–Taylor pulsar, 1974 onward) or direct detection. In 1936 he and Rosen briefly argued that the waves did not exist.

claim.label: A triumph of the theory
claim.summary: Speculative. Lorentz worked on general relativity and admired it.
voice: I have spent part of my life on the equations of this theory. That they should be confirmed at such a distance, and by such a small effect, is the kind of result that makes an old man glad he chose physics.
claim.reasoning: Speculative; grounded in his documented work on general relativity.

claim.label: A real world, measured
claim.summary: Speculative; grounded in Planck's documented realism.
voice: Here is the real world, doing exactly what our laws require of it, a billion light-years away and long before anyone looked. I take that as a small argument for the view I defended against Mach.
